capacious

kuh-PAY-shus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Capacious means roomy enough to hold or contain a very great deal, with plenty of open space inside.

The old theater's capacious lobby swallowed the entire crowd without ever feeling full, its marble floor stretching well past the last row of coat racks.

Example

The walk-in closet was so capacious that it held her entire wardrobe, three suitcases, and a full-length mirror, with room left over to stand and dress comfortably in the middle.

Capacious means having a large interior space able to hold a great deal. It's not just big on the outside (a solid boulder can be huge yet hold nothing); it's specifically about how much open room there is inside to contain things. The closet swallowing a whole wardrobe plus suitcases and still leaving space to move is exactly what capacious describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

spacious: Spacious means offering plenty of open room and stresses an open, airy feel. Capacious is more specific: it measures how much something can hold or take in, so a capacious bag may not look spacious at all from the outside.

commodious: Commodious means roomy in a comfortable, convenient way — a commodious cabin is pleasant to settle into. Capacious says nothing about comfort; it stresses pure holding power, the sheer amount that fits inside.

voluminous: Voluminous describes something bulky and large in outward volume, like a voluminous cloak that spreads wide around the wearer. Capacious looks inward instead, at the room something offers for holding things — a case can be slim outside yet capacious within.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cramped: Uncomfortably small, with too little room to hold or move — the direct opposite of capacious, which describes generous interior space that holds a great deal.

confined: Restricted to a tight, closed-in space with no room to spare — the reverse of the open, take-anything-in roominess that capacious describes.

Where it sits · how much open space it offers — snug → roomy → capacious

snug vs. capacious: Snug sits at the small end of the scale: a snug reading nook fits one person cozily, while a capacious library hall could take in hundreds of readers and all their books.

roomy vs. capacious: A roomy apartment gives you comfortable space to live in, but a capacious warehouse loft goes further — it could swallow the furniture of three apartments and still feel open.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — cap-

Root — cap-: to take, hold, contain (Latin capere)

Suffix — -acious

Suffix — -acious: tending to, abounding in (Latin -ax, adjective-forming, + -ious)

Put it together

Put it together: Start with the Latin root cap-, from capere, 'to take, hold, contain.' Now add the adjective-forming suffix -acious, meaning 'tending to' or 'abounding in' — the same ending you hear in tenacious ('tending to hold on') and audacious ('tending to dare'). Put them together and capacious literally means 'tending to take things in' — the Romans' own adjective was capax, 'able to hold much.' That's exactly what the word still describes today: something with so much open room inside that it can take in and hold a great deal.

Use the root in a new word: capture

Use the root in a new word: capture: The rangers set a humane trap to capture the escaped parrot — to capture is literally to 'take hold of' something, straight from the same Latin root capere.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Capacious is a formal, somewhat literary word, at home in descriptive writing about buildings, vehicles, containers, and even the mind ('a capacious memory'). In everyday speech, say 'roomy' or 'big inside,' but reach for capacious when you want to emphasize that something holds an impressively great deal.
